I’m sorry—I don’t have live‑internet access from within this environment, so I can’t pull up current or future weather forecasts directly for those coordinates right now. However, I can show you exactly how you could obtain that information yourself using a free or paid weather API service. --- ### How to Get Hourly Forecasts for 10 Days at 37.8651 N / –119.5383 W | Step | What You Need | Example Code | |------|---------------|--------------| | **1** | Sign up for a weather‑data provider that offers hourly forecasts out to 10+ days.
Popular choices:
  • [OpenWeatherMap](https://openweathermap.org/api/one-call-api) – Free tier gives 48h + 7d daily
  • [Visual Crossing Weather](https://www.visualcrossing.com/weather-data-editions)
  • [NOAA Climate Data Online](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/) – US‑only, requires token
| *No coding needed* | | **2** | Obtain your API key/token after registration.| *No coding needed* | | **3** | Build the request URL. For most services you’ll supply latitude (`lat`), longitude (`lon`) and optionally units (`units=metric` or `imperial`).
Example for Visual Crossing (free tier):
`https://weather.visual-crossing.com/VisualCrossingWebServices/rest/services/timeline/37.8651,-119.5383/next10days?unitGroup=metric&include=hours%2Cprecipitation&key=YOUR_API_KEY`| ```python
# Using requests to hit the endpoint\nimport requests, json\nurl = \"https://weather.visual-crossing.com/VisualCrossingWebServices/rest/services/timeline/37.8651,-119.5383/next10days\"\nparams = {\n \"unitGroup\": \"metric\", # change to imperial for °F & mph\n \"include\": \"hours,precipitation\",\n \"key\": \"YOUR_API_KEY\" # replace with your own key\n}\nresponse = requests.get(url, params=params)\ndata = response.json()\nprint(json.dumps(data, indent=2))\n``` | #### What the JSON Response Looks Like (abridged) ``` { "address": "...", "resolvedAddress": "...", "timezone": "...", "utcOffset": ..., "forecastInfo": { … }, "locations": { "37.8651,-119.5383": { "datetimeEpoch": ..., "temp": 12.5, ... "hourly": [ {"datetimeEpoch": ..., "temp": 13.0, "windspeed": 8.2, "precipType":"rain","precipAccumulation":0}, {...} ] } } } ``` Each entry inside `"hourly"` contains: | Field | Meaning | |-------|---------| | `datetimeEpoch` | Unix timestamp for that hour | | `temp` | Temperature (°C or °F depending on unit group) | | `windspeed` | Wind speed (m/s or km/h/mph) | | `precipType` | “none”, “rain”, “snow”… | | `precipAccumulation` | Amount of precipitation during that hour (mm/cm/mm?) | Repeat the same pattern for each day until you’ve covered all ten days. --- ### Quick Alternative: NOAA’s GFS Model (Free, but more complex) If you’re comfortable parsing raw NetCDF files, NOAA’s Global Forecast System provides high‑resolution hourly data out to ~16 days. Steps: 1. Download the latest GFS run file (e.g., `gfs.t00z.pgrbf01.f000.nc`). 2. Use libraries such as `netcdf4`, `xarray`, or `cf-python`. 3. Extract variables: - `air_temperature_isobaric_surface_850_hPa` → temp - `u_wind_component_of_air_velocity_at_height_above_ground_level_10_meters` → u-wind - `v_wind_component_of_air_velocity_at_height_above_ground_level_10_meters` → v-wind - `total_precipitable_water` or `convective_rain_rate`. This route yields very detailed physics‑based predictions but demands significant preprocessing effort. --- ### Summary Because I can’t make outbound HTTP calls myself, I recommend trying the Visual Crossing or OpenWeatherMap One Call API—both give easy-to‑parse JSON containing hourly temperatures, windspeeds, and precipitation types for up to 10–15 days. Plug in the coordinates above, add your personal API key, and parse the returned JSON into whatever format suits your project. If you’d like sample scripts for other languages (JavaScript, R, etc.) just let me know!
